subject: physics
question_text: Show that the trajectory of a projectile is a parabola. Derive expressions for its time of flight, maximum height and horizontal range.

verification.note: Sources: the Sri Chaitanya IPE Junior Fastrack (Rev. May 2024) carries this material as TWO three-star SHORT ANSWER questions of Unit 4 — ***2 (maximum height and range) and ***4 (trajectory is a parabola) — and the chapter has no LONG ANSWER section at all. The 8-mark LAQ here combines them the way the paper asks the full question; the 4-mark cut is the book’s ***2 exactly. BOTH mark splits are invented, as is the choice of which steps the 4-mark answer may omit. A Telangana IPE teacher must confirm both before a student sees them. No exam appearance years are printed for Unit 4, so appearances[] stays empty.

cuts.label: 8-mark answer
cuts.note: The full question as the paper asks it: parabola, then time of flight, height and range. The 8-mark split is a claim.

cuts.label: 4-mark answer
cuts.question_text: Show that the maximum height and the horizontal range of a projectile are u²sin²θ/2g and u²sin2θ/g.

cuts.note: Sri Chaitanya Fastrack SHORT ANSWER ***2 of Unit 4, three-star. The 4-mark split and the decision to fold the time of flight into the range step are invented.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Define projectile
lines: A body thrown into space at an angle with
the horizontal, moving under gravity alone,
is called a projectile.
Air resistance is neglected.
steps.margin_note: Say "under gravity alone". The examiner looks for that phrase, and for air resistance being neglected.
steps.why: Two facts the whole derivation rests on are hidden in this sentence: no horizontal force, and a constant vertical acceleration g. State them and every later line follows.
common_mistakes: Writing "thrown at 90 degrees" — a straight-up throw is not this case.
Leaving out that air resistance is neglected.

recall.must_convey: That a projectile is a body thrown at an angle to the horizontal that moves under gravity alone.
accept: a body thrown at an angle to the horizontal
it moves only under gravity
projectile definition, thrown at an angle, only gravity acts

body projected at an angle, air resistance neglected

steps.label: Draw the figure
steps.margin_note: Label O, A, B, the angle θ, both components, H and R. One mark is for a complete, labelled figure.
steps.why: Every later line names a point from this figure — A is where the vertical velocity is zero, B is where y returns to zero. Without them the examiner cannot follow H or R.
common_mistakes: Drawing the path as an arc of a circle instead of a parabola.
Marking H at the end of the path instead of at the top.
Leaving the angle θ unmarked at O.

recall.must_convey: That a figure is drawn at this point. Naming the act of drawing is full credit.

steps.label: Resolve u
lines: Let the body be projected from O with
speed u at an angle θ to the horizontal.

lines.text: Along x:  u cos θ,   acceleration = 0
Along y:  u sin θ,   acceleration = −g

steps.margin_note: Both components come from the one speed u. The horizontal one never changes; only the vertical one does.
steps.why: Projectile motion is two ordinary straight-line motions happening at once. Splitting u is what lets you use the equations of motion you already know, one axis at a time.
common_mistakes: Swapping sin and cos between the two axes.
Giving the horizontal motion an acceleration.

recall.must_convey: That u is resolved into u cos theta horizontally and u sin theta vertically, with zero horizontal acceleration and −g vertically.
accept: resolve u into u cos theta and u sin theta
horizontal component u cos theta, vertical component u sin theta
along x there is no acceleration, along y it is minus g
components ni resolve chestha
split the velocity into horizontal and vertical parts
reject: time of flight is two u sin theta by g

steps.label: Equation of the path
lines: Let the body be at P(x, y) after time t.
Along x, the velocity is constant:
Along y, with acceleration −g:

lines.text: y = (u sin θ) t − ½ g t²

lines: Substituting for t:

lines.text: y = x tan θ − g x² / (2u² cos²θ)

lines: Here tan θ and g/(2u²cos²θ) are constants,
which is the equation of a parabola.
steps.margin_note: Eliminate t between the two equations. Two of the eight marks are for this step, so show the substitution.
steps.why: x and y each depend on time, so neither alone shows the shape of the path. Removing t leaves a relation between x and y only — and that relation is what a parabola is.
common_mistakes: Stopping at x and y separately without eliminating t.
Dropping the minus sign and getting an upward curve.
Not saying that A and B are constants, which is the whole point.

recall.must_convey: That t is eliminated between x and y to give y in terms of x alone, of the form y = Ax − Bx², a parabola.
accept: substitute t from the x equation into the y equation
eliminate t and you get y equals A x minus B x squared
y in terms of x only, so it is a parabola
t ni eliminate chesi parabola vasthundi
the equation of the trajectory is a parabola
reject: maximum height is u squared sin squared theta by two g
range is u squared sin two theta by g
heard_as: a x minus b x squared

steps.label: Time of flight
lines: At the landing point B the body is back
at the same level, so y = 0 at t = T.

lines.text: 0 = (u sin θ) T − ½ g T²
½ g T = u sin θ

steps.margin_note: T is the time for the WHOLE path. The time to the top is half of it.
steps.why: The range needs a time to multiply by, and this is it. Setting y back to zero is what picks out the landing instant rather than any other moment.
common_mistakes: Using the time to the top instead of the whole flight in the range.
Cancelling T without saying T is not zero.

recall.must_convey: That y = 0 at landing gives T = 2u sin theta / g.
accept: put y equals zero at the end to get the time of flight
time of flight is two u sin theta by g
at B the displacement is zero so T equals two u sin theta over g
time of flight T ni theesukunta
the total time in the air
reject: maximum height is u squared sin squared theta by two g
range equals horizontal velocity into time
heard_as: two u sin theta by g

steps.label: Maximum height
lines: At the highest point A the vertical
velocity is zero.
steps.margin_note: Use only the VERTICAL velocity here. The horizontal one is still u cos θ at the top, and it is not zero.
steps.why: The top is defined by the vertical velocity reaching zero — that single condition is what turns the equation of motion into a formula for H.
common_mistakes: Setting the whole velocity to zero at the top instead of only the vertical part.
Using u instead of u sin θ in v² − u² = 2as.

recall.must_convey: That the vertical velocity is zero at the top, giving H = u² sin²θ / 2g.
accept: at the top the vertical velocity is zero
maximum height is u squared sin squared theta by two g

reject: range is u squared sin two theta by g
time of flight is two u sin theta by g

steps.label: Horizontal range
lines: The horizontal velocity never changes, so

lines.text: R = (u cos θ)(2u sin θ / g)
R = 2u² sin θ cos θ / g

lines: and since sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ,
steps.margin_note: Box the final result. Write the sin 2θ line — the marked answer is in that form, not in sin θ cos θ.
steps.why: Horizontal motion has no acceleration, so distance is simply speed times time. The double-angle step is what puts the answer in the form the question asks for.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as 2u² sin θ cos θ / g.
Using the time to the top instead of the full time of flight.

recall.must_convey: That R = horizontal velocity × time of flight = u² sin 2θ / g.
accept: range is horizontal velocity into time of flight
range equals u squared sin two theta by g

using sin two theta equals two sin theta cos theta

heard_as: u squared sin two theta by g

steps.label: Special cases (extra)
lines: R is maximum when sin 2θ = 1,
that is when θ = 45°.
Two angles θ and (90° − θ) give the same R.
steps.margin_note: Not asked. Write it only if time is left.
steps.why: These two facts are the fastest check on your own formula, and each is a starred very-short question in its own right.
common_mistakes: Claiming 45° also gives the maximum height — it does not.
